name: 50 Ways to Leave Your Guava Burger

recipe.history:
Guava (Psidium guajava) is a tropical fruit native to the Americas, believed to have originated in the region stretching from southern Mexico through Central America and into northern South America, with strong culinary roots in Brazil, Cuba, Puerto Rico, and Colombia. Archaeological evidence suggests indigenous peoples of the Americas were cultivating and consuming guava thousands of years before European contact. When Spanish and Portuguese colonizers arrived in the 15th and 16th centuries, they encountered a fruit so adaptable and abundantly sweet that they carried it with them across trade routes to Africa, Southeast Asia, and the Indian subcontinent. Today, India is the world's largest producer of guava, yet the fruit's soul remains deeply tied to the Caribbean and Latin American traditions that first elevated it — from the beloved guava paste (pasta de guayaba) of Cuban bakeries to the bright, rose-tinged jellies of Brazilian mercados.

Guava made its slow and fragrant migration into American cuisine largely through Caribbean and Latin American immigrant communities settling in Florida, New York, and California throughout the 20th century. Cuban-American bakeries in Miami's Little Havana brought guava paste and cream cheese pastries (pastelitos de guayaba) into the American mainstream, and chefs began experimenting with guava as a savory counterpoint — its floral sweetness and mild tartness making it a natural companion to grilled and smoked meats. The rise of chef-driven burger culture in the 2000s and 2010s, which embraced global flavors and farm-to-table ingredient sourcing, opened the door for guava to appear as glazes, chutneys, and sauces atop handcrafted beef patties. Restaurants in Miami, Los Angeles, and New York began pairing guava with sharp cheeses, pickled onions, and spiced aiolis, discovering that the fruit's complexity could transform a simple burger into something genuinely memorable.

I remember the first time I tasted something close to this burger — it was at a small window-service spot in Little Havana, the kind of place with a handwritten menu taped above a pass-through and a single ceiling fan working twice as hard as it should have been. The cook handed me a grilled pork sandwich slathered in guava sauce, and the sweetness hit me before I even bit into it — that warm, floral smell that's somewhere between strawberry and pear but entirely its own thing. I ate it standing on the sidewalk in the afternoon heat, juice running down my wrist, and I thought: this is what summer tastes like when someone actually loves you. Years later, when I started making burgers seriously, I kept chasing that feeling. The 50 Ways to Leave Your Guava Burger is my answer to it — the memory of that afternoon folded into a brioche bun with a pink, yielding patty and a sauce that smells like somewhere warm.

Cooking a burger to medium rare — an internal temperature of 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) — is not a preference; it is the correct answer to a question most people are still getting wrong. At medium rare, the fat within a well-chosen beef blend has begun to render but has not been driven out entirely, leaving the patty juicy, tender, and genuinely flavorful rather than a gray disk of compacted protein. The Maillard reaction has done its work on the exterior crust, producing depth and complexity, while the interior retains the faint pink blush that signals the meat has been treated with respect. A burger cooked beyond this point — to medium well or well done — loses its moisture irreversibly, its texture tightens, and the nuance of a quality blend disappears beneath the taste of heat and regret. If you are using fresh, quality ground beef from a trusted source, there is no safety argument strong enough to justify overcooking it into submission. Medium rare is not bravado; it is the only temperature at which a burger can tell you everything it has to say.
ingredients: 3 large eggs (2 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
600g freshly ground beef blend — 60% chuck (80/20), 40% short rib
1 tsp flaky sea salt (for seasoning, applied just before cooking)
1–2 chipotle peppers in adobo sauce, minced
1 small garlic clove, minced to a paste
1 large red onion, thinly sliced into half-moons
4 thick slices sharp white cheddar or aged Manchego
instructions: 1. Make the pickled onions first (they need at least 1 hour): Combine warm water, apple cider vinegar, sugar, and salt in a jar or bowl and stir until dissolved. Add the sliced red onions, press them down to submerge, and let sit at room temperature for a minimum of 1 hour. Refrigerate if making ahead — they keep for up to 2 weeks.

2. Make the brioche dough: In the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the dough hook, combine bread flour, yeast, sugar, and salt. Whisk briefly to distribute. Add the warmed milk, warm water, and 2 eggs. Mix on low speed until a shaggy dough forms, about 2 minutes.

3. Increase mixer speed to medium and knead the dough for 5 minutes. With the mixer running on medium-low, add the softened butter one cube at a time, waiting for each piece to be incorporated before adding the next. Once all butter is added, increase to medium-high and knead for 8–10 more minutes until the dough is smooth, elastic, and pulls cleanly from the sides of the bowl.
4. Transfer dough to a lightly oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and let rise at room temperature until doubled, approximately 1 to 1.5 hours.

5. Once risen, turn the dough out onto a lightly floured surface and divide into 4 equal portions (approximately 150g each). Shape each portion into a tight ball by folding the edges under and rolling against the surface. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, spacing them at least 3 inches apart. Cover loosely with oiled plastic wrap and let proof for 45–60 minutes until puffed and pillowy.

6. Preheat your oven to 375°F / 190°C. Beat the remaining egg with 1 tbsp water to make an egg wash. Gently brush the tops of the proofed buns and sprinkle with sesame seeds if using. Bake for 16–18 minutes until deep golden brown. Transfer to a wire rack to cool completely before slicing.

7. Make the guava sauce: Combine the cubed guava paste, orange juice, apple cider vinegar, honey, grated ginger, smoked paprika, cayenne, and salt in a small saucepan over medium-low heat. Cook, stirring frequently, until the guava paste has completely melted and the sauce is smooth and glossy, about 8–10 minutes. If the sauce is too thick, add orange juice one tablespoon at a time. Taste and adjust seasoning — it should be sweet, tangy, and gently spiced. Remove from heat and let cool slightly.

8. Make the chipotle aioli: Combine mayonnaise, minced chipotle peppers, adobo sauce, lime juice, and garlic paste in a small bowl. Stir well, taste, and add salt as needed. The aioli should be smoky, creamy, and have a mild heat. Cover and refrigerate until ready to use.

9. Prepare the beef patties: Remove your ground beef from the refrigerator 20 minutes before cooking to take the chill off. Divide into 4 equal portions of approximately 150g each. Using your hands, gently form each portion into a patty roughly 4 inches in diameter and 3/4 inch thick. Press a slight dimple in the center of each patty with your thumb — this prevents the patty from doming as it cooks. Do not overwork the meat. Season both sides generously with flaky sea salt and cracked black pepper immediately before cooking.

10. Heat a cast iron skillet or heavy griddle over high heat until it begins to smoke. Add a thin film of neutral oil with a high smoke point (such as avocado or grapeseed oil). Place the patties in the pan without crowding — cook in batches if necessary. Sear without moving for 2.5–3 minutes until a deep, dark crust forms on the bottom.

11. Flip the patties once. Immediately lay a slice of cheese over each patty. Cook for an additional 2–2.5 minutes. Begin checking the internal temperature using an instant-read thermometer — you are targeting 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. This is not negotiable. At this temperature the fat is rendered, the center is pink and yielding, and the burger is at the peak of everything it can be. Remove from heat and rest on a wire rack for 3 minutes — the carry-over cooking will bring it to the ideal final temperature.

12. Toast the buns: While the patties rest, slice each brioche bun in half. Butter the cut sides generously with unsalted butter and place face-down on the still-hot skillet over medium heat. Toast for 60–90 seconds until golden and slightly crisp at the edges.

13. Assemble the burgers: Spread a generous layer of chipotle aioli on the bottom bun. Layer with a leaf of butter lettuce, followed by 2–3 slices of avocado. Place the rested, cheese-crowned patty on top. Spoon 2–3 tablespoons of warm guava sauce generously over the cheese and patty, letting it drape down the sides. Top with a small tangle of pickled red onions. Crown with the top bun.
14. Serve immediately — the guava sauce should still be warm, the cheese barely melted, and the patty resting at that perfect, rosy medium rare. Serve with nothing that will distract from it.
